docs.title: Installation
docs.text:

uv add complexipy

Git for the diff options

The --diff, --diff-only, and --staged options require Git 2.30 or newer on your PATH. Check your version with git --version. Git is not required for analysis without these options.

docs.title: What is Cognitive Complexity?
docs.text:
Cognitive complexity measures how hard a function's control flow is to follow. Use it to keep code easy to review and change, whether a person or an AI agent wrote it.

These two functions have the same cyclomatic complexity, 4. Their cognitive complexity is different:

Flat: score 3Nested: score 6 
def example1(a, b, c):
    if a:        # +1
        return 1
    if b:        # +1
        return 2
    if c:        # +1
        return 3
    return 4

def example2(a, b, c):
    if a:        # +1
        if b:    # +2 (1 + nesting_level)
            if c:  # +3 (1 + nesting_level)
                return 1
    return 4

Nested code makes the reader hold more context, so each nesting level adds to the score. complexipy implements the Cognitive Complexity metric by G. Ann Campbell for Python. How scores are calculated

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
# Analyze the current directory
complexipy .

# Set a custom threshold
complexipy . --max-complexity-allowed 10

# Show failing functions with refactor suggestions
complexipy . --failed --suggest-refactors

# Save results to JSON
complexipy . --output-format json

# Block regressions against a git reference
complexipy . --diff main

# Exclude paths with glob patterns
complexipy . --exclude "tests/**"

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from complexipy import file_complexity

# Analyze a file
result = file_complexity("app.py")
print(f"File complexity: {result.complexity}")

for func in result.functions:
    print(f"{func.name}: {func.complexity}")

docs.title: Origins and Inspiration
docs.text:
complexipy is inspired by the Cognitive Complexity research paper by G. Ann Campbell from SonarSource. This groundbreaking work introduced a new approach to measuring code complexity that better aligns with human understanding.

Independent Project

While complexipy implements the cognitive complexity methodology described in Campbell's research, it is not affiliated with or endorsed by SonarSource or Sonar products. complexipy is an independent, open-source implementation written in Rust for Python code analysis.

docs.title: Why Cognitive Complexity?
docs.text: Cyclomatic complexity measures code structural, testing, and branch density (number of paths) by counting decision points. However, this doesn't reflect how humans actually understand code. Cognitive complexity measures how difficult code is for humans to understand and maintain by penalizing nesting, flow breaks, and human-unfriendly logic.

docs.title: Different Approaches to Measuring Complexity
docs.text:
Cyclomatic complexity (McCabe, 1976) counts every decision point:

# Cyclomatic complexity: 4
def example1(a, b, c):
    if a:
        return 1
    if b:
        return 2
    if c:
        return 3
    return 4

# Cyclomatic complexity: 4 (same as above!)
def example2(a, b, c):
    if a:
        if b:
            if c:
                return 1
    return 4

Both functions have the same cyclomatic complexity, but any developer will tell you example2 is much harder to understand.

docs.title: The Cognitive Complexity Solution
docs.text:
Cognitive complexity accounts for nesting:

# Cognitive complexity: 3
def example1(a, b, c):
    if a:        # +1
        return 1
    if b:        # +1
        return 2
    if c:        # +1
        return 3
    return 4

# Cognitive complexity: 6
def example2(a, b, c):
    if a:        # +1
        if b:    # +2 (1 + nesting_level)
            if c:  # +3 (1 + nesting_level)
                return 1
    return 4

This aligns with human intuition: nested code requires holding more context in your mind.

docs.title: Adopting complexipy in an Existing Codebase
docs.text:
A codebase that already has complex functions fails the first run. This guide adds complexipy without fixing everything first: record what exists, block anything new or worse, then reduce the backlog over time.

The output on this page comes from a run on the Flask source tree with the default threshold of 15.

docs.title: 1. See the current state
docs.text:
List the most complex functions:

complexipy src --top 5

src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py
    Blueprint::register 29  ❌  FAILED

src/flask/app.py
    Flask::make_response 26  ❌  FAILED
    Flask::url_for 22  ❌  FAILED

src/flask/cli.py
    find_best_app 18  ❌  FAILED
    find_app_by_string 17  ❌  FAILED

A plain complexipy src exits with code 1 here, so it cannot run in CI yet.

docs.title: 2. Record a baseline
docs.text:
complexipy src --snapshot-create

No function fails the run. 10 functions above 15 are ALLOWED: no worse than the baseline the gate compares with.
Snapshot watermark passed. Baseline stored at ./complexipy-snapshot.json

Commit complexipy-snapshot.json. From now on, every run reads it: a function in the snapshot passes while it does not get more complex, and a function that improves leaves the snapshot. See Snapshot Baselines.

docs.title: 3. Block new and worse functions
docs.text:
Run the same command in CI, without --snapshot-create. A new function above the threshold fails the run:

src/flask/helpers.py
    merge_headers 23 (new, Δ = +23)  ❌  FAILED

To review only what a branch changes, compare it with the target branch:

complexipy src --diff origin/main

+--------+-------------------------------------+-----------+-------+
| Status | Location                            | Change    | Gate  |
+==================================================================+
| NEW    | src/flask/helpers.py::merge_headers | 23  (new) | FAILS |
+--------+-------------------------------------+-----------+-------+

Net: 1 new
Gate: 1 function fails: REGRESSED or NEW above the threshold.

See CI/CD Integration for the GitHub Action, the pre-commit hook, and GitLab, and Complexity Diff for the diff options.

docs.title: 4. Show scores in the editor
docs.text: The language server shows the score of each function above the threshold as you type, so a function gets attention before it reaches CI. Set inlay-hints = "always" in the language server settings to show the score of every function. See Editor Integration for VS Code, Neovim, and Zed.

docs.title: 5. Reduce the backlog
docs.text:
Ask for refactor suggestions on the failing functions:

complexipy src --failed --suggest-refactors

Preview the fixes that complexipy can apply by itself, then apply them:

complexipy src --fix --dry-run
complexipy src --fix

Fixed C002 at src/flask/helpers.py:684-694 (-4 complexity)
Skipped C001 at src/flask/helpers.py:684-694 (not safe to auto-apply)

Here merge_headers went from 23 to 19. The skipped suggestion needs a manual change. See Refactoring Rules for what each rule does and which ones --fix applies.

docs.title: 6. Lower the threshold
docs.text: When the backlog is small, set a lower max-complexity-allowed in your configuration file and record the baseline again with --snapshot-create. Repeat in small steps. See Configuration and Understanding Scores for the recommended thresholds.

docs.title: AI Agent Workflows
docs.text:
Coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex CLI write code in a loop: edit files, run tools, and continue from the output. Cognitive complexity measures how hard that code is to review, and a function over the limit is cheapest to fix while the agent still has the file in context, if something tells the agent about it.

Hooks are commands an agent runs at lifecycle events. A hook that runs complexipy puts the analysis in the same turn, before a human reads the diff. This page shows two hooks for both agents: one after each file edit, one when the agent tries to finish.

docs.title: What the hooks use from complexipy
docs.text:
complexipy exits with status 1 when a function is above max-complexity-allowed, and 0 when the code passes. A hook maps that exit code to the agent's feedback protocol, so the hook itself stays small.

The recipes check the diff instead of the whole repository:

  • complexipy <file> --diff HEAD checks the edited file on each edit.
  • complexipy . --diff main checks the branch when the turn ends.

Each hook passes the report to the agent as its feedback. --failed --plain --suggest-refactors keeps it short: one path:line function complexity line per function over the limit, and one line per refactor plan with its rule id, title, and reduction:

complexipy src/app.py --diff HEAD --failed --plain --suggest-refactors --max-complexity-allowed 15

src/app.py:3 nested 6
  C007 Merge 3 nested if statements (-4)

The diff table follows, and so does the list of functions that an ignore comment the change added now hides, so an agent cannot pass the check by adding # complexipy: ignore.

The scripts are POSIX sh and expect complexipy on the PATH. They work in git repositories, because --diff needs a reference to compare against.

Both hooks compare with a git reference: the edit hook checks the uncommitted changes of the file the agent edited, and the Stop hook checks the whole branch against main. Start the agent from a clean tree, or commit or stash your own work, so the feedback is about the agent's changes.

docs.title: The edit hook
docs.text:
Save this script in the hook directory of your agent and make it executable:

#!/bin/sh
limit=${COMPLEXIPY_MAX_COMPLEXITY:-15}
ref=${COMPLEXIPY_EDIT_DIFF_REF:-HEAD}
file=$(sed -n 's/.*"file_path"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' | head -n 1)
case "$file" in
    "") target=. ;;
    *.py) target=$file ;;
    *) exit 0 ;;
esac
root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
cd "$root" || exit 0
if ! git rev-parse --verify --quiet "$ref^{commit}" >/dev/null; then
    printf '%s\n' "complexipy hook: the git reference '$ref' does not exist." >&2
    exit 1
fi
report=$(complexipy "$target" --diff "$ref" --failed --plain --suggest-refactors \
    --max-complexity-allowed "$limit" --color no 2>&1)
status=$?
if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
    exit 0
fi
if [ "$status" -ne 1 ]; then
    printf '%s\n' "complexipy could not check the edit (exit $status):" "$report" >&2
    exit 1
fi
printf '%s\n' "complexipy: the edit adds or worsens a function above the cognitive complexity limit of $limit." "$report" "Refactor the functions listed above." >&2
exit 2

The script reads tool_input.file_path from the hook input on stdin, skips a file that is not Python, and checks only that file. When the input names no file, as with a Codex apply_patch edit, it checks every uncommitted change. Exit status 2 is the feedback signal for both agents: Claude Code shows the stderr text to the model, and Codex CLI replaces the tool result with it.

docs.title: The end-of-turn hook
docs.text:
Save this script next to the edit hook:

#!/bin/sh
limit=${COMPLEXIPY_MAX_COMPLEXITY:-15}
ref=${COMPLEXIPY_DIFF_REF:-main}
if grep -Eq '"stop_hook_active"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*true'; then
    exit 0
fi
root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
cd "$root" || exit 0
if ! git rev-parse --verify --quiet "$ref^{commit}" >/dev/null; then
    printf '%s\n' "complexipy hook: the git reference '$ref' does not exist." >&2
    exit 1
fi
report=$(complexipy . --diff "$ref" --failed --plain --suggest-refactors \
    --max-complexity-allowed "$limit" --color no 2>&1)
status=$?
if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
    exit 0
fi
if [ "$status" -ne 1 ]; then
    printf '%s\n' "complexipy could not check the branch (exit $status):" "$report" >&2
    exit 1
fi
printf '%s\n' "complexipy: the branch adds or worsens a function above the cognitive complexity limit of $limit." "$report" "Refactor the functions listed above before you finish." >&2
exit 2

It compares the branch with main and runs again whenever the agent tries to stop. A failing status sends the agent back to work with the message; a passing one lets the turn end. The script reads stop_hook_active, so it blocks at most once per turn. Set COMPLEXIPY_DIFF_REF when your base branch is not main, and COMPLEXIPY_MAX_COMPLEXITY when you use a different limit. The edit hook takes its own reference from COMPLEXIPY_EDIT_DIFF_REF (default HEAD), which helps when the agent commits after each edit.

A Stop hook fires at the end of every response, not only when the task is complete, so the check runs on each turn and blocks when the branch adds or worsens a function above the limit.

Both agents pass stop_hook_active in the hook input. The script exits 0 while that flag is true, which keeps a Stop hook from blocking forever. Claude Code also cuts a Stop hook after eight consecutive blocks.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Copy both scripts to .claude/hooks/ in the repository and make them executable:

chmod +x .claude/hooks/complexipy-edit.sh .claude/hooks/complexipy-stop.sh

Add both events to .claude/settings.json. If the file already has a hooks object, add these entries as siblings of the existing event keys:

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|MultiEdit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/complexipy-edit.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/complexipy-stop.sh",
            "timeout": 120
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Claude Code normally reloads hooks when the settings file changes; restart the session if a new hook does not appear. Run /hooks to confirm both appear under PostToolUse and Stop.

Claude Code runs project hooks only after you trust the workspace.

To test a hook without an agent turn, pipe the input the event sends on stdin and check the exit code:

echo '{"hook_event_name":"Stop","stop_hook_active":false}' | .claude/hooks/complexipy-stop.sh

Exit 0 lets the turn end, and exit 2 blocks the stop and passes the message to the agent. See the Claude Code hooks reference for the event fields and the exit code rules, and the hooks guide for more examples.

docs.title: Codex CLI
docs.text:
Copy both scripts to .codex/hooks/, then create .codex/hooks.json:

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "apply_patch|Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "sh \"$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/complexipy-edit.sh\"",
            "timeout": 120,
            "statusMessage": "Checking cognitive complexity"
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "sh \"$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/complexipy-stop.sh\"",
            "timeout": 120,
            "statusMessage": "Checking cognitive complexity"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The commands resolve the scripts from the git root because Codex can start in a subdirectory. Codex runs a project hook only after you trust the project .codex layer and review the hook with /hooks, and it asks again when the hook changes. The same hooks can be declared inline in .codex/config.toml under [[hooks.PostToolUse]] and [[hooks.Stop]] if you prefer one file. See the Codex hooks reference for the full schema and the trust rules.

docs.title: Recipes without hooks
docs.text:
The same verdict works outside the agent loop:

  • Gate the branch in pre-commit or CI with complexipy . --diff main --max-complexity-allowed 15; see CI/CD.
  • Ask for a plan with complexipy <path> --suggest-refactors, review the patch with complexipy <path> --fix --dry-run, and apply it with --fix.
  • Record the rule in the instruction file the agent reads (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md): "Keep every function at or below 15 cognitive complexity. Before you finish, run complexipy . --diff main --max-complexity-allowed 15 and refactor anything it flags."
  • Point the editor at the language server when the agent reads diagnostics; see Editor Integration.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The path:line form, the refactor plan lines in --plain, and the list of ignore comments a change adds need 9.0.0 or newer. With 8.3.0, the hooks give the same exit codes, and the feedback shows path function complexity lines and the diff table.
  • When a tool needs structured data instead of text, --output-format json --output - (9.0.0 or newer) writes the report to stdout. Each entry carries line_start, line_end, and line_complexities, the lines that add to the score.
  • The hooks treat exit 1 as a limit breach, and complexipy also exits 1 for some configuration errors. When the feedback does not match a function in the diff, read the message at the end of the feedback.
  • --diff needs Git 2.30 or newer. Each hook checks first that its git reference exists. When it does not, for example when the default branch is master, the hook exits 1 with a message that names the reference; set COMPLEXIPY_DIFF_REF or COMPLEXIPY_EDIT_DIFF_REF to a reference that exists.
  • Hooks run with your permissions. Review the scripts before you commit them to a repository, like any other command a tool executes for you.
  • The scripts need a POSIX shell. On Windows, install Git for Windows, which provides sh, and make sure the agent finds it on the PATH.
  • Hook formats change between agent releases. The examples follow the references linked above, and the scripts need no change when the configuration schema moves.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
The complete Python API exposed by complexipy. Import everything from the complexipy package. For usage examples, see the Python API section below.

# Core functions
file_complexity(path: str, check_script: bool = False, no_ignore: bool = False, with_plans: bool = True) -> FileComplexity
code_complexity(source: str, check_script: bool = False, no_ignore: bool = False, with_plans: bool = True) -> CodeComplexity
collect_all_ignored_locations(paths: List[str], exclude: List[str], invocation_path: str = ".") -> Tuple[List[IgnoredLocation], List[str]]
collect_removable_ignored_locations(paths: List[str], exclude: List[str], max_complexity_allowed: int, invocation_path: str = ".") -> Tuple[List[RemovableIgnore], List[str]]
compute_diff(current_files: List[FileComplexity], git_ref: str, invocation_path: Optional[str] = None) -> List[DiffEntry]
has_regressions(entries: List[DiffEntry], max_complexity: int) -> bool

# Return types
FileComplexity:
  ├─ path: str (relative to the working directory, or absolute when outside it)
  ├─ file_name: str
  ├─ complexity: int
  └─ functions: List[FunctionComplexity]

FunctionComplexity:
  ├─ name: str
  ├─ complexity: int
  ├─ line_start: int
  ├─ line_end: int
  ├─ line_complexities: List[LineComplexity]
  └─ refactor_plans: List[RefactorPlan]

RefactorPlan:
  ├─ kind: str
  ├─ title: str
  ├─ line_start: int
  ├─ line_end: int
  ├─ column_start: int
  ├─ current_complexity: int
  ├─ estimated_reduction: int
  ├─ estimated_complexity_after: int
  ├─ rule_id: str
  ├─ category: RuleCategory
  ├─ applicability: Applicability
  ├─ description: str
  ├─ explanation: str
  ├─ references: List[str]
  ├─ suggestion: Optional[CodeSuggestion]
  ├─ help: Optional[str]
  └─ doc_url: str

CodeSuggestion:
  ├─ replacement: str
  ├─ applicability: Applicability
  ├─ description: str
  └─ insertions: List[CodeInsertion]

CodeInsertion:
  ├─ before_line: int
  └─ text: str

RuleCategory: Complexity | Readability
Applicability: MachineApplicable | MaybeIncorrect | Informational

LineComplexity:
  ├─ line: int
  └─ complexity: int

IgnoredLocation:
  ├─ path: str
  ├─ line: int
  └─ comment: str

CodeComplexity:
  ├─ complexity: int
  └─ functions: List[FunctionComplexity]

DiffEntry:
  ├─ file_path: str
  ├─ func_name: str
  ├─ old_complexity: Optional[int]
  ├─ new_complexity: Optional[int]
  └─ status: DiffStatus (property)

DiffStatus: REGRESSED | IMPROVED | UNCHANGED | NEW | REMOVED

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: file_complexity raises ValueError when the file cannot be read or decoded as UTF-8, or does not parse. code_complexity raises ValueError when the code does not parse. An internal error inside any analysis function also surfaces as ValueError, so one except ValueError skips a file that cannot be analyzed.

docs.title: Analyzing Files
docs.text:
from complexipy import file_complexity

# Analyze a file
result = file_complexity("src/main.py", check_script=True)

print(f"Total complexity: {result.complexity}")
print(f"File path: {result.path}")

# Iterate over functions
for func in result.functions:
    print(f"{func.name}:")
    print(f"  Complexity: {func.complexity}")
    print(f"  Lines: {func.line_start}-{func.line_end}")

# Analyze without honoring inline ignore comments
result = file_complexity("src/main.py", no_ignore=True)

docs.title: Analyzing Code Strings
docs.text:
from complexipy import code_complexity

# Analyze code snippet
code = """
def calculate_discount(price, customer):
    if customer.is_premium:
        if price > 100:
            return price * 0.8
        else:
            return price * 0.9
    return price
"""

result = code_complexity(code, check_script=True)
print(f"Complexity: {result.complexity}")

for func in result.functions:
    print(f"{func.name}: {func.complexity}")

# Analyze code string without honoring ignore comments
result = code_complexity(code, no_ignore=True)

Both functions build refactor plans by default. Pass with_plans=False when you only need the scores: refactor_plans stays empty and the analysis skips the plan work.

result = file_complexity("src/main.py", with_plans=False)

docs.title: Comparing Against a Git Reference
docs.text:
compute_diff compares current complexity results against a git reference (commit, tag, or branch) and returns DiffEntry objects - one per function that changed, appeared, or disappeared. has_regressions reports whether any entry breaches a complexity threshold (a REGRESSED or NEW function above max_complexity). The entries carry no function bodies, so a moved or renamed function counts as NEW; only --diff, which compares the bodies, lets an exact copy through. Each file is read from the git repository that holds it, at its own path, and a submodule at the commit its outer repository pins, as with --diff, so a file moved since the reference reports its functions as NEW: its old path is not among the files you pass. Like --diff, it needs Git 2.30 or newer on your PATH. invocation_path, the working directory by default, anchors relative file paths and plays the role of the directory a CLI run starts in.

from complexipy import (
    compute_diff,
    has_regressions,
    file_complexity,
    DiffEntry,
    DiffStatus,
)

# Analyze the current state of the files you care about
current = [file_complexity(p) for p in changed_files]

# Compare against a git reference (the working directory is the default cwd)
entries = compute_diff(current, "origin/main")

# Filter for regressions above your threshold
regressions = [
    e
    for e in entries
    if e.status == DiffStatus.REGRESSED and e.new_complexity > 15
]

# Or use the ratchet gate directly (fails on REGRESSED/NEW above threshold)
if has_regressions(entries, 15):
    raise SystemExit("Complexity regressions detected")

DiffEntry exposes file_path, func_name, old_complexity, and new_complexity (either may be None for NEW / REMOVED functions), plus the status property. status is a DiffStatus member - a str-based enum, so it compares equal to its string value (e.g. DiffStatus.REGRESSED == "REGRESSED").

for e in entries:
    if e.status != DiffStatus.UNCHANGED:
        print(f"{e.file_path}::{e.func_name}: {e.status} "
              f"{e.old_complexity} -> {e.new_complexity}")

docs.title: Practical API Usage
docs.text:
Example: Pre-commit Hook

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check complexity of staged Python files."""
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from complexipy import file_complexity

MAX_COMPLEXITY = 15

def main():
    # Get staged Python files (integrate with git)
    staged_files = get_staged_python_files()

    violations = []
    for filepath in staged_files:
        result = file_complexity(str(filepath))

        for func in result.functions:
            if func.complexity > MAX_COMPLEXITY:
                violations.append({
                    'file': filepath,
                    'function': func.name,
                    'complexity': func.complexity,
                    'line': func.line_start
                })

    if violations:
        print("Complexity violations found:")
        for v in violations:
            print(f"  {v['file']}:{v['line']} - "
                  f"{v['function']} (complexity: {v['complexity']})")
        sys.exit(1)

    print("All functions pass complexity check!")
    sys.exit(0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Example: Code Quality Dashboard

from pathlib import Path
from complexipy import file_complexity
import json

def analyze_project(root_path: str):
    """Generate complexity report for entire project."""
    project = Path(root_path)
    results = []

    for py_file in project.rglob("*.py"):
        if "venv" in str(py_file) or ".venv" in str(py_file):
            continue

        try:
            result = file_complexity(str(py_file))
            results.append({
                'file': str(py_file),
                'complexity': result.complexity,
                'functions': [
                    {
                        'name': f.name,
                        'complexity': f.complexity,
                        'line_start': f.line_start,
                        'line_end': f.line_end
                    }
                    for f in result.functions
                ]
            })
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Error analyzing {py_file}: {e}")

    # Sort by complexity
    results.sort(key=lambda x: x['complexity'], reverse=True)

    # Save report
    with open("complexity-report.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(results, f, indent=2)

    # Print summary
    total_files = len(results)
    total_complexity = sum(r['complexity'] for r in results)
    avg_complexity = total_complexity / total_files if total_files else 0

    print(f"Analyzed {total_files} files")
    print(f"Total complexity: {total_complexity}")
    print(f"Average complexity: {avg_complexity:.2f}")

    # Top 10 most complex files
    print("\nTop 10 most complex files:")
    for r in results[:10]:
        print(f"  {r['file']}: {r['complexity']}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    analyze_project("./src")

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: This page documents how the current Rust CLI compares to the 7.0.1 Python CLI. Both versions share the same Rust analysis engine; the difference is the CLI pipeline: argument parsing, config resolution, path walking, and output rendering now run in Rust, and the Python interpreter no longer does any analysis work. The environment block below names the exact version and commit.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• New CLI: built from the repository with uv run maturin develop --release, invoked as .venv/bin/complexipy.
  • Baseline CLI: complexipy==7.0.1 installed from PyPI with uv add into an isolated project, invoked as its venv's bin/complexipy.
  • Invocation parity: both CLIs run as bare console scripts with byte-identical flags, each workload from its own empty directory. The uv run wrapper is excluded from timing so neither side pays uv process overhead.
  • Corpus: real open-source repos, shallow-cloned at pinned commits, plus a single-file probe that isolates interpreter and CLI startup from tree analysis.
  • Metrics: wall time via hyperfine (warmup 3, 5 runs; probe warmup 5, 20 runs) with stdout discarded; peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l, 3 runs, maximum reported.
  • Parity gate: before timing, both CLIs export JSON for the requests repo and the single-file probe. The exit codes match, and every function the baseline reports has the same score in the new CLI, so both sides score the same code. The new CLI also scores functions defined under a module-level if or try, which 7.0.1 skips.

The benchmark is repeatable:

bash benchmarks/benchmark-cli.sh

docs.title: What the numbers say
docs.text:
• Large trees win the most. django (~2900 files, its test suite included) is roughly 68-91x faster: the Rust engine analyzes the tree in parallel across all cores, where the Python CLI processed it on one.
  • Small and medium trees (requests, flask) are roughly 9-15x faster.
  • Startup is cheaper. The single-file probe is about 3.3x faster, which is the Python interpreter + typer/rich import cost removed from the hot path.
  • The scaling table at the bottom of the results measures the Rust engine on a synthetic fixture at 1x, 2x, and 4x sizes. Ratios near 2 mean linear scoring; ratios near 4 mean quadratic behavior. The recorded ratios sit near 1.0-1.2.
  • Output rendering is cheaper too. Rendering the full results table on django costs ~0.02 s on the Rust CLI against ~5.7 s on the Python CLI (the default minus --quiet delta), so the wall-clock gap widens on large trees when results are actually printed - the [render] rows measure that path end to end.
  • Peak memory is lower on small trees and higher on large ones. The Rust CLI uses 3-5 MB less on requests and flask and about 13 MB less on the single-file probe, because the Python interpreter and its display libraries are gone from the process. On django it peaks about 60 MB higher: it analyzes files in parallel and allocates with mimalloc, which trade memory for speed.

  • pylint-cognitive-complexity runs as a pylint plugin with every other check disabled. pylint uses one core by default.
