docs.title: Configuration Priority
docs.text:
complexipy loads configuration in this order (highest to lowest priority):

  1. Command-line arguments
  2. complexipy.toml
  3. .complexipy.toml
  4. pyproject.toml (under [tool.complexipy])

complexipy reads the first of these files that parses and has valid values, and never merges files. When a higher file shadows a lower one that also holds settings, a warning names the file that is not applied.

--isolated ignores every configuration file, and --config <path> reads only the named file: its [tool.complexipy] section when the file is named pyproject.toml, and the whole file otherwise. Use either one in CI to pin the gate, so a change to the repository's configuration cannot change it.

A configuration file that is not a regular file, that is larger than 4 MiB, or that is a symlink resolving outside the directory is skipped with a warning. A configuration error names the file, the line and column, or the key, and never repeats the file's contents.

Values read from a configuration file are checked before use: paths, output, and cache-dir must stay inside the directory complexipy runs from, symlinks included, and a diff branch cannot start with -. Pass a path outside the project on the command line instead. output = "-" writes the single selected format to stdout.

docs.title: Example Configurations
docs.text:
complexipy.tomlpyproject.toml.complexipy.toml 
paths = ["src", "tests"]
max-complexity-allowed = 10
exclude = ["migrations/**", "build/**"]
snapshot-create = false
snapshot-ignore = false
quiet = false
ignore-complexity = false
failed = false
color = "auto"
sort = "asc"
output-format = ["json", "gitlab"]
output = "reports/"
check-script = false
no-ignore = false
report-ignored = false
force-exclude = false
cache-dir = ".complexipy_cache"

[tool.complexipy]
paths = ["src", "tests"]
max-complexity-allowed = 10
exclude = ["migrations/**", "build/**"]
failed = true
sort = "desc"
check-script = true
cache-dir = ".complexipy_cache"

# Hidden config file for team-specific settings
max-complexity-allowed = 15
exclude = ["venv/**", ".venv/**", "node_modules/**"]
cache-dir = ".complexipy_cache"

check-script is supported in TOML. --top and --plain are CLI-only flags.

docs.title: JSON Schema
docs.text:
complexipy.schema.json, at the root of the repository, describes every key of the configuration, with its type, default, and description. A TOML language server such as Taplo (Even Better TOML in VS Code) uses it for completion, hover text, and validation. The schema is in the SchemaStore catalog, so such an editor finds it for complexipy.toml, .complexipy.toml, and [tool.complexipy] in pyproject.toml with no setup. If your editor does not read SchemaStore, add this line at the top of complexipy.toml or .complexipy.toml:

#:schema https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rohaquinlop/complexipy/main/complexipy.schema.json

The schema rejects unknown keys, so the editor marks a typo such as max-complexity-alowed. complexipy itself ignores unknown keys.

docs.title: Diff Configuration
docs.text:
The comparison policy can be declared once in the repository instead of passing the same flags on every call. Add a [tool.complexipy.diff] section to the same configuration file:

complexipy.tomlpyproject.toml 
[diff]
branch = "main"
staged = true

[tool.complexipy.diff]
branch = "main"
staged = true
  • branch sets the default reference for --diff and --diff-only. A plain complexipy . then behaves like complexipy . --diff main, enforcement included. Pass --diff <ref> or --diff-only <ref> to override the reference for a single run.
  • staged enables staged comparison by default, like passing --staged on every call.
  • CLI flags always take precedence over the section values.
  • branch = "" disables the diff for the current repository (opt-out), and the section's staged value with it.
  • A [diff] section changes what the exit code checks, so every run it applies to prints a warning on stderr that names the file. Pass --diff, --isolated, or --config <path> to pin the gate in CI.
  • Resolution order: CLI flag, then the diff section.
  • If the configured branch does not exist in the local clone (for example a fresh or shallow clone), every function reports as NEW, the enforcement still applies, and the run prints a warning that names the reference and the repository. Fetch the branch or pass --diff <ref> with an existing reference instead.

docs.title: Language Server Settings
docs.text:
The language server reads the same configuration files as the CLI, from the workspace root, plus an lsp section that controls what the editor shows:

complexipy.tomlpyproject.toml 
max-complexity-allowed = 15
exclude = ["migrations/**"]

[lsp]
inlay-hints = "threshold"
per-line-hints = false
diagnostics = true
diagnostic-range = "name"
hover = "signature"
workspace-diagnostics = false

[tool.complexipy]
max-complexity-allowed = 15
exclude = ["migrations/**"]

[tool.complexipy.lsp]
inlay-hints = "threshold"
per-line-hints = false
diagnostics = true
diagnostic-range = "name"
hover = "signature"
workspace-diagnostics = false
Key Description Default inlay-hints threshold shows the per-function hint only above max-complexity-allowed, always shows it for every function, never suppresses every hint threshold per-line-hints Also show the complexity added by each line, as +2. Lines that add nothing are skipped false diagnostics Publish a warning for every function above max-complexity-allowed true diagnostic-range What the warning underlines: name the function name, or function the whole function name hover Where hover answers: signature on the def lines, function on any line of the function, or never signature workspace-diagnostics Also publish warnings for files that are not open, from a scan of the workspace folder false

The server reads the top-level max-complexity-allowed, paths, exclude, select, ignore, and no-ignore keys, and it ignores every other key of the same file: quiet, failed, sort, color, output, output-format, cache-dir, snapshot-create, snapshot-ignore, ignore-complexity, check-script, report-ignored, force-exclude, and diff. A function whose complexity equals the threshold passes, as it does on the command line.

docs.title: Cache Configuration
docs.text:
complexipy stores per-function complexity data between runs to power delta/diff comparisons. By default this cache lives in .complexipy_cache/ inside your invocation directory. Instead of the default location you can redirect it to any directory which is useful for CI, shared cache directories or avoiding polluting the project tree.

# CLI flag (highest priority)
complexipy . --cache-dir .cache/complexipy

Or declare it once in a configuration file:

complexipy.tomlpyproject.toml.complexipy.toml 
cache-dir = ".cache/complexipy"

[tool.complexipy]
cache-dir = ".cache/complexipy"

cache-dir = ".cache/complexipy"

docs.title: Complexity Diff
docs.text:
The --diff, --diff-only, and --staged options require Git 2.30 or newer on your PATH. Check your version with git --version. Git is not required for analysis without these options.

Compare current results against any git reference:

complexipy . --diff HEAD~1
complexipy . --diff main
complexipy src/ --max-complexity-allowed 10 --diff HEAD~1

By default --diff enforces the complexity threshold: the run exits with code 1 only when a change breaches the contract relative to --max-complexity-allowed:

  • A new function introduced above the threshold.
  • A modified function whose complexity increased and ends above the threshold (including already-over functions that get worse).

Functions that regress but stay at or below the threshold (e.g. 3 → 4 with --max-complexity-allowed 15) are not failures.

To see the diff visually without affecting the exit code, use --diff-only instead:

complexipy . --diff-only HEAD~1

To compare the staged (git index) content instead of the working tree - "what complexity am I about to commit?" - add --staged:

# Staged changes vs HEAD (the default baseline for --staged)
complexipy . --staged

# Staged changes vs a specific ref
complexipy . --diff main --staged

Like --diff, --staged enforces the threshold against the staged content and fails when a staged change pushes a function above --max-complexity-allowed. It compares only the staged files the run selects: the path arguments, paths, and exclude apply as they do without --staged, to the index rather than the working tree, so a staged regular file is compared whatever the working tree holds at its path. Staged deletions that discovery would have selected produce REMOVED entries: under a selected directory, outside hidden paths, and not matched by exclude, .gitignore, .ignore, or git's exclude file. Staged additions produce NEW entries. Use --diff-only with --staged for a visual-only view.

A rename or a move passes the gate as long as the function's body stays as it was. A file that git pairs as renamed compares with its old path when the run covers that path; a file moved in from outside the selected paths compares as added, and a file moved out of them reports nothing. A path that was not a regular file at the reference, such as a symbolic link, is not read there: it compares as added, and its deletion reports nothing. A function above the threshold that the change adds passes only when it replaces a REMOVED function with the same body and at least its complexity, each removed function replaced once, and the compared files do not hold more functions with that body than they did at the reference. The complexity matters because a call to a function's own name scores as recursion, so a rename can make the same body more complex. The compared files are the ones the diff compares: modified, renamed from a covered path, deleted from a covered path, and added. Bodies compare structurally, ignoring formatting and comments, and leave out the name, the decorators, and the parameters, so a function rename, a class rename, a move to another file, and a method that becomes a function all pass, while a function that moves and changes fails. Functions that an ignore comment hides count on both sides, so a function copied from one that is now hidden fails. Bodies count and pair only within the repository that holds each file, since each repository is compared at its own reference. The diff table names, in a Gate column, the REMOVED function with the same body that each passing function replaces. A function that an ignore comment now hides was not removed, so it does not report as REMOVED. A deleted Python file that discovery would have selected reports its functions as REMOVED, so a function moved out of it passes as well.

When --diff or --staged decides the exit code, the report shows the gate's verdict. A function that fails the run, REGRESSED or NEW above the threshold, is listed as FAILED and marked FAILS in the diff table's Gate column, and the table ends with a Gate: line that counts them. A function above the threshold that the gate lets through is listed as ALLOWED, and --failed lists only the functions that fail the run. A snapshot run lists the functions its snapshot lets through as ALLOWED too.

Below the diff table, the report lists each function that an ignore comment hides now but did not hide at the reference: a comment added to an existing function, or a new function added with one. Each line gives path:line, the function, and its score with the comment disregarded. The list informs a reviewer and never changes the exit code. A function renamed or moved while it kept its comment is listed too, since the name it is hidden under is new. --quiet hides the list, as it hides the table.

This requires git and a repository-backed path. --diff and --diff-only read each file from the repository that holds it, so a run from outside the repository compares against the same history as a run from inside it. A submodule, meaning a repository that the repository around it tracks as a gitlink in its index, is read at the commit that the outer repository pins for it at the reference, and deeper nesting follows each pin in turn. When the run starts inside the submodule, it is read at the reference itself. A repository inside another that the outer one does not track is read at the reference, like any other repository. --staged uses the repository of the working directory; outside a repository it prints a warning and compares nothing, so the report lists functions above the threshold as FAILED but the threshold does not decide the exit code. When a file sits outside any repository, the reference names no commit in the file's repository, or the outer repository pins no commit for the submodule at the reference, or pins a commit the submodule does not have, every function of that file reports as NEW and the run prints a warning that names the cause. The functions of a file that does not parse at the reference report as NEW too.

Instead of repeating the reference on every call, declare the comparison policy once in a configuration file - see Diff Configuration.

docs.title: Snapshot Baselines
docs.text: Snapshots allow you to adopt complexipy gradually in large, existing codebases.

docs.title: Creating a Snapshot
docs.text:
complexipy . --snapshot-create --max-complexity-allowed 15

This creates complexipy-snapshot.json in your working directory, recording all functions that currently exceed the threshold.

Create the baseline from the command line. snapshot-create = true in a configuration file re-records the baseline on every run, so every current violation passes; such a run prints a warning on stderr that names the file.

docs.title: How Snapshots Work
docs.text:
Once a snapshot exists, complexipy will:

  • ✅ Pass: Functions that were already in the snapshot and haven't gotten worse
  • ✅ Pass: Functions that improved (automatically removed from snapshot)
  • ❌ Fail: New functions that exceed the threshold
  • ❌ Fail: Functions above the threshold that moved to another file or got a new name. The snapshot keys each entry by file and name, so run --snapshot-create after such a change to record them again
  • ❌ Fail: Tracked functions that got more complex

docs.title: Using Snapshots in CI
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/complexity.yml
name: Complexity Check

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
    check:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4

            - name: Install complexipy
              run: pip install complexipy

            - name: Check complexity
              run: complexipy . --max-complexity-allowed 15

The snapshot file (complexipy-snapshot.json) should be committed to version control.

docs.title: Ignoring Snapshots
docs.text:
Temporarily disable snapshot checking:

complexipy . --snapshot-ignore

Use this when:

  • Refactoring multiple files at once
  • Regenerating the baseline
  • Testing different thresholds

docs.title: Snapshot File Format
docs.text:
[
    {
        "path": "src/legacy.py",
        "file_name": "legacy.py",
        "functions": [
            {
                "name": "old_function",
                "complexity": 23
            }
        ]
    }
]

Snapshots are stored as a JSON array of analyzed files. Each entry contains only functions above the threshold at the time the snapshot was written. The file is rewritten after successful snapshot checks, so improved functions are removed automatically. Updates only touch the files analyzed in the run - entries for files outside the analysis are preserved, so running on a subset of files (for example through a pre-commit hook) never shrinks the baseline. Entries for files that no longer exist are dropped when the file is rewritten. Snapshots created by older complexipy versions may need to be regenerated with --snapshot-create.

Functions of one file that share a name, such as a property's getter and setter, get separate entries: the first in source order keeps the name, and the next ones are stored as name#2, name#3. --diff keys its comparison the same way.

docs.title: Editor Integration
docs.text:
complexipy ships a Language Server Protocol (LSP) server, so your editor can surface the same cognitive complexity analysis the CLI produces while you write code. The server runs the same Rust engine as complexipy and the Python API, and it needs no configuration to start being useful: install complexipy, point your editor at complexipy lsp, and keep working.

Inside the editor you get:

  • Inlay hints - the cognitive complexity of a function, shown at the end of its def line as cognitive: 18.
  • Hover - hovering the def lines of a function shows its name, its cognitive complexity, whether it exceeds the allowed threshold, and the title of the top refactoring suggestion when one exists.
  • Diagnostics - one warning per function above max-complexity-allowed, with the message cognitive complexity 18 exceeds the allowed 15 on the function name.
  • Code actions - every refactoring suggestion for a function above max-complexity-allowed. A suggestion that is safe to apply is a quick fix that rewrites the buffer in one undoable edit. The others appear in the refactor menu with their help text.

Results refresh as you type. The server uses full document sync and, by default, analyzes only the documents you have open, so there is no workspace-wide scan unless lsp.workspace-diagnostics is on, and no need to save.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install complexipy so that the complexipy command is on your PATH:

uv tool install complexipy

or, with pip:

pip install complexipy

Anything that installs the complexipy command works. The editor starts the server as a subprocess with complexipy lsp; no separate binary download exists. Upgrade the tool with uv tool upgrade complexipy or pip install --upgrade complexipy to pick up new rules and settings.

docs.title: Neovim
docs.text:
Neovim 0.11 and later can configure and enable the server with vim.lsp.config and vim.lsp.enable:

vim.lsp.config("complexipy", {
  cmd = { "complexipy", "lsp" },
  filetypes = { "python" },
  root_markers = { "complexipy.toml", ".complexipy.toml", "pyproject.toml", ".git" },
})

vim.lsp.enable("complexipy")

On Neovim 0.10, start the server directly instead:

vim.lsp.start({ name = "complexipy", cmd = { "complexipy", "lsp" } })

Inlay hints are opt-in in Neovim. Enable them once, globally:

vim.lsp.inlay_hint.enable(true)

or per buffer with vim.lsp.inlay_hint.enable(true, { bufnr = 0 }).

docs.title: Zed
docs.text:
Zed starts a language server only when Zed or an extension registers it. The complexipy extension lives in the zed/ folder of the repository. Until it is published in the Zed extension registry, install it as a dev extension:

  1. Clone https://github.com/rohaquinlop/complexipy.
  2. Run zed: install dev extension from the command palette and select the zed/ folder.

Then enable the server and inlay hints for Python in settings.json:

{
  "inlay_hints": { "enabled": true },
  "languages": {
    "Python": {
      "language_servers": ["complexipy", "..."]
    }
  }
}

The "..." entry keeps every other Python language server you already use enabled. If your settings already list Python language servers without "...", add "complexipy" to that list, or Zed does not start it.

Zed turns inlay hints off by default. inlay_hints.enabled turns them on for every language server, so type hints from servers such as ty or basedpyright appear next to the complexipy hint.

The lsp.hover and lsp.diagnostic-range settings apply in Zed as well. The colored badges of the VS Code extension do not: Zed shows the inlay hints.

The extension runs complexipy lsp from the PATH. To use another binary, set its path:

{
  "lsp": {
    "complexipy": {
      "binary": {
        "path": "/full/path/to/complexipy",
        "arguments": ["lsp"]
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
Install the complexipy extension from the Visual Studio Marketplace, or from OpenVSX in VSCodium and other forks. It is a client of complexipy lsp: it starts the server for Python files and shows its inlay hints, hover, and warnings. VS Code shows inlay hints by default, so no editor setting is needed.

The extension also adds a status bar item with the number of functions over the threshold in the active file. Click it to open the Problems panel.

To see colored badges instead of inlay hints, set complexipy.display to decorations. The extension then shows ƒ N after every function declaration and +N after every line that adds complexity, in green, yellow, or red:

  • A function is green up to half of max-complexity-allowed, yellow up to the limit, and red above it.
  • A line is yellow from complexipy.decorations.lineWarningAt (default 3) and red from complexipy.decorations.lineErrorAt (default 5).
{
  "complexipy.display": "decorations",
  "complexipy.decorations.lineWarningAt": 3,
  "complexipy.decorations.lineErrorAt": 5
}

The badges show every function and every line that adds complexity, whatever inlay-hints and per-line-hints say. They need complexipy 8.2.0 or later. With an older server the extension shows a warning and keeps the inlay hints.

The extension runs complexipy lsp from the PATH. To use another binary, set its path in settings.json:

{
  "complexipy.server.path": "/full/path/to/complexipy"
}

A relative path resolves against the first workspace folder. In Restricted Mode, VS Code ignores a complexipy.server.path set in the workspace's settings, so an untrusted repository cannot choose the binary; the extension then runs the path from your user settings, or complexipy from the PATH.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The server reads the same configuration files as the CLI - complexipy.toml, .complexipy.toml, or pyproject.toml (under [tool.complexipy]) - discovered at the root of each workspace folder:

complexipy.tomlpyproject.toml 
max-complexity-allowed = 15

[lsp]
inlay-hints = "threshold"   # "always" | "threshold" | "never"
per-line-hints = false
diagnostics = true
diagnostic-range = "name"   # "name" | "function"
hover = "signature"         # "signature" | "function" | "never"
workspace-diagnostics = false

[tool.complexipy]
max-complexity-allowed = 15

[tool.complexipy.lsp]
inlay-hints = "threshold"   # "always" | "threshold" | "never"
per-line-hints = false
diagnostics = true
diagnostic-range = "name"   # "name" | "function"
hover = "signature"         # "signature" | "function" | "never"
workspace-diagnostics = false
Key Default Description max-complexity-allowed 15 Functions strictly above this value are reported. A function at the limit passes. exclude [] Glob patterns, matched relative to the workspace folder that holds the configuration file and to each of its paths entries. Excluded files produce no hints and no diagnostics. no-ignore false Analyze functions even when an inline ignore comment suppresses them. paths [] Folders that exclude and lsp.workspace-diagnostics work from, relative to the workspace folder. Empty means the workspace folder itself. select all rules Refactoring rules or rule groups the server suggests, as in Rule Selection. ignore [] Refactoring rules or rule groups the server never suggests. Wins over select. lsp.inlay-hints "threshold" When to show the per-function hint: "threshold", "always", or "never". lsp.per-line-hints false Also show a +N hint on every line with a non-zero complexity increment. lsp.diagnostics true Publish warnings for functions above max-complexity-allowed. lsp.diagnostic-range "name" What the warning underlines: "name" the function name, or "function" the whole function. lsp.hover "signature" Where hover answers: "signature" on the def lines, "function" on any line of the function, or "never". lsp.workspace-diagnostics false Also publish warnings for files that are not open. The server scans the workspace folder, or its paths entries, with the same file discovery as complexipy, and follows changes on disk when the editor watches files.

The server ignores every other key of the same file: quiet, failed, sort, color, output, output-format, cache-dir, snapshot-create, snapshot-ignore, ignore-complexity, check-script, report-ignored, force-exclude, and diff. Run those keys through complexipy <path>.

The server reads the configuration again when you save a change to one of these files at the root of a workspace folder. The editor must support dynamic registration of workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles. If a saved file does not parse, the editor shows a warning and the folder uses the default settings. With an editor that does not watch files, restart the server after you change the configuration.

docs.title: Inlay hints
docs.text:
The hint is placed at the end of the last line of the function declaration: the line that closes the signature. For a single-line signature that is the def line, and for a decorated function it is the def line rather than the @decorator line above it. For a signature that spans several lines the hint sits after the closing ) or )::

def heavy(
    a,
    b,
):

Here the hint sits at the end of the ): line.

  • inlay-hints = "threshold" (the default) shows the per-function hint (cognitive: 18) only when the function is above max-complexity-allowed.
  • inlay-hints = "always" shows it for every function.
  • inlay-hints = "never" suppresses every hint, including per-line hints.
  • per-line-hints = true additionally shows a +N hint at the end of every line that has a non-zero complexity increment. Lines with an increment of zero never produce a hint.

The server reports the same functions complexipy <path> reports: top-level functions, plus methods of classes. A function nested inside another one is folded into its parent, so there is no separate hint for it. With hover = "function", hovering inside a nested function therefore shows its parent.

docs.title: Hover
docs.text:
• hover = "signature" (the default) answers only on the declaration lines: from the def line to the line that closes the signature. Hovering a call in the body leaves the editor's own hover alone.
  • hover = "function" answers on any line of the function.
  • hover = "never" turns hover off.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
• diagnostics = false publishes no warnings at all.
  • diagnostic-range = "name" (the default) underlines only the function name on its def line. diagnostic-range = "function" underlines the whole function.
  • The reported threshold matches complexipy <path>: a function whose complexity equals max-complexity-allowed passes. Only strictly greater values are reported, as cognitive complexity 18 exceeds the allowed 15.
  • A document the parser cannot read produces exactly one warning with the code complexipy-parse-error on the range where the parser fails, with the parser's message. While that warning is present, hints and hover keep answering from the last text that parsed, so the file does not go blank while you type. The warning clears itself as soon as the document parses again.
  • Each warning links to Understanding Scores, so the entry in the Problems panel opens the explanation of the score.

docs.title: Quick fixes
docs.text:
Code actions answer for every function above max-complexity-allowed that the requested range touches, with one action per refactoring suggestion, up to five per function. The title names the rule and the reduction, as C007: Merge nested if statements (-1). An estimated reduction reads (~5, not measured).

  • A suggestion that complexipy --fix would apply is a quick fix. Applying it sends one edit over the changed lines, so one undo reverts it. The first such suggestion of a function is the preferred fix.
  • Any other suggestion, such as a help-only rule like C003, is a disabled refactor action, and its help text is the reason. It never edits the buffer. Editors hide disabled actions from the automatic quick fix menu, so look for it in the refactor menu: Refactor... (Ctrl+Shift+R) in VS Code.
  • A document that does not parse offers no actions until it parses again.

docs.title: Ignores and exclusions
docs.text:
• exclude globs are matched relative to the workspace folder that holds the configuration file, and relative to each paths entry of that file, the same way a CLI run in that folder matches them. Excluded files produce no hints and no diagnostics.
  • A nested workspace folder without a configuration file of its own uses the configuration of the nearest enclosing folder that has one.
  • A pattern that can never match, such as ./vendor/** or vendor/, is reported as a warning.
  • A malformed glob is reported once per configuration load and skipped. Each configuration problem (a malformed glob, an oversized list, an unknown rule id in select or ignore, a selection that leaves no rule active, or a file that does not parse) is written to the server log, and the editor shows one fixed warning that points to that log. The warning never quotes the configuration, so a repository cannot place a link in it. The other patterns in the list keep applying.
  • A list too large to compile as one program is reported once per configuration load and still applied one pattern at a time. A CLI run stops on the same list.
  • Inline suppression comments (# noqa: complexipy and # complexipy: ignore) are honored exactly as in the CLI, unless no-ignore = true.

docs.title: The editor cannot find the complexipy command
docs.text:
The editor starts the server as a subprocess, so complexipy must be on the PATH that the editor process inherits. Point the server at an absolute path when the tool is installed somewhere the editor cannot see:

  • Neovim: set cmd = { "/full/path/to/complexipy", "lsp" }.
  • Zed: set "path" to the absolute binary in the lsp.complexipy.binary block. Without it, the extension looks for complexipy on the PATH, and Zed shows an error when it is not there.
  • VS Code: set complexipy.server.path to the absolute binary. Without it, the extension looks for complexipy on the PATH, and VS Code shows an error when it is not there.

Alternatively, start it through uv without installing anything globally:

cmd = { "uvx", "complexipy", "lsp" },

docs.title: Where to read the server logs
docs.text:
The server never writes anything except protocol frames to stdout; all logging goes to stderr. Read it where your editor collects it:

  • Neovim: :LspLog.
  • Zed: open the log panel from the command palette (zed: open log).
  • VS Code: open the Output panel and select the complexipy channel.

docs.title: Hints do not appear
docs.text: Inlay hints are opt-in in most editors. Enable them in the editor itself (vim.lsp.inlay_hint.enable(true) in Neovim, "inlay_hints": { "enabled": true } in Zed), and remember that the default inlay-hints = "threshold" only shows the hint when a function is above max-complexity-allowed. Set inlay-hints = "always" to see every function.

docs.title: The whole file shows warnings
docs.text: A limit lower than expected usually means the wrong configuration is active. The server reads complexipy.toml, .complexipy.toml, or pyproject.toml from the root of the document's workspace folder; check that the folder the editor opened is the one holding your settings. The server reads the file at startup, and again when you save it in an editor that watches files for the server. In other editors, restart the server after you edit it (:LspRestart in Neovim, editor: restart language server in Zed).

docs.title: Per-line hints do not appear
docs.text: per-line-hints is off by default. Set it to true to add the +N hints.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
The --diff ratchet checks and the exit-code gates remain CLI-only. The language server is meant to guide you while you write, not to replace the CI contract, so existing CI usage is unchanged.

Other limits of the current server:

  • The server analyzes Python documents only. A document whose language is not python and whose path does not end in .py produces no hints and no warnings.
  • The server declares full document sync, so it expects the whole buffer on every change. A change that carries a range is ignored, and one line is written to the server log.
  • In a workspace with several folders, each folder reads its own configuration file. A document uses the deepest folder that contains it, and a document outside every folder uses the first folder. Folders that the editor adds or removes take effect without a restart.
  • The initializationOptions of the client are ignored. Settings come from the configuration file.
  • The lsp word reserves the first command-line argument: complexipy lsp starts the server. To analyze a file or directory named lsp, run complexipy -- lsp. On a terminal the server prints that hint when a path named lsp exists.

docs.title: Rule Selection
docs.text:
Refactoring rules carry ids like C001 (see Refactoring Rules). Two flags choose which rules are active, and both accept comma-separated lists and repeat:

Flag Effect --select C001,C007 Report only the listed rules --ignore C007 Never report the listed rules --select complexity Report only the rules of one group --ignore readability Never report the rules of one group

A group name stands for every rule of that category, as listed in Refactoring Rules: complexity or readability. Group names mix with rule ids, as in --select complexity,C007.

With no flag every rule is active. When both flags name the same rule, --ignore wins. Rule ids and group names are case-insensitive. An unknown id prints a warning on stderr that it matches no registered rule. A select list keeps narrowing the active set even when one of its ids is unknown, and a second warning says so when select and ignore leave no rule active.

The same keys work in complexipy.toml, .complexipy.toml, and pyproject.toml:

select = ["C001", "C007"]
ignore = ["C002"]

A toml value may also be one comma-separated string, like the flags: select = "C001, C007".

A flag replaces the toml key it names. Rule selection never changes the exit code: the exit code follows the complexity threshold, snapshots, paths, and diff gating only. A rule that is not active never appears in the terminal, the refactor plans, JSON, CSV, SARIF, or GitLab output.

docs.title: Inline Ignores
docs.text:
Suppress complexity warnings for specific functions using the # complexipy: ignore comment:

def complex_legacy_function():  # complexipy: ignore
    # Complex logic that can't be refactored yet
    pass

# Or with a reason
def another_complex_function():  # complexipy: ignore (technical debt: issue #123)
    pass

The ignore comment can also be placed on the line above the function definition:

# complexipy: ignore
def complex_function():
    pass

A marker counts only inside a comment: on the def line, on a line of its signature or decorators, or as a comment on its own line directly above. The same text in a string, a docstring, or a decorator argument, or a trailing comment on the code line above, suppresses nothing. The words are matched whole and separated by spaces or tabs only, so # complexipy: ignored is not a marker.

docs.title: Suppressing Specific Rules
docs.text:
Add a bracketed rule list to keep the function but hide the named rules:

def tangled(a, b):  # complexipy: ignore[C007]
    pass

The function is still analyzed and reported; only the listed rules are suppressed for it. Separate several ids with commas: # complexipy: ignore[C001,C007]. The # noqa: complexipy[C007] form behaves the same way. A bare marker keeps suppressing the whole function. Bracketed text that is not a list of rule ids is a reason, so # complexipy: ignore [technical debt] keeps suppressing the whole function. Group names are not rule ids here: # complexipy: ignore[readability] also suppresses the whole function.

Deprecated Syntax

The # noqa: complexipy syntax is deprecated and will be removed in a future version. Please migrate to # complexipy: ignore instead.

Why? Tools like yesqa automatically strip # noqa comments that aren't recognized by flake8, which would silently remove your complexipy suppressions. The new syntax avoids this conflict entirely.

Use Sparingly

Inline ignores should be temporary. Document why the complexity is necessary and track technical debt.

docs.title: Disabling Inline Ignores
docs.text:
Use --no-ignore to disregard all inline ignore comments and analyze every function:

complexipy . --no-ignore

Functions previously suppressed by # complexipy: ignore or # noqa: complexipy will be analyzed normally and may fail the threshold.

docs.title: Reporting Ignored Functions
docs.text:
Use --report-ignored to list every location where an ignore comment suppresses a function:

# List ignored functions
complexipy . --report-ignored

# Combine with --no-ignore to report while analyzing everything
complexipy . --report-ignored --no-ignore

Each location prints as path:line # comment-text, followed by the count. When --output-format json is also active, ignored locations are exported to complexipy-ignored.json. --quiet hides the list, and the JSON export is still written. With --output -, the file is written to the directory complexipy runs from.

Both flags are also available in the Python API via no_ignore=True:

from complexipy import file_complexity, code_complexity

# Analyze without honoring ignore comments
result = file_complexity("app.py", no_ignore=True)

To programmatically collect ignored locations, use collect_all_ignored_locations():

from complexipy import collect_all_ignored_locations

locations, failed = collect_all_ignored_locations(
    paths=["src"],
    exclude=["tests/**"],
)
for loc in locations:
    print(f"{loc.path}:{loc.line}  {loc.comment}")

docs.title: Removing Stale Ignore Comments
docs.text:
An ignore comment is only necessary while the suppressed function's complexity exceeds --max-complexity-allowed. Once the function's complexity drops to or below the limit, the comment is stale and can be removed. complexipy detects this automatically on every run and reports the locations to clean up:

complexipy .

Example output:

The following ignore comment(s) are no longer necessary (complexity is within the allowed limit) and can be removed:
src/legacy.py:42  function=parse_legacy_config complexity=8  # complexipy: ignore

The report is purely informational: it never affects the exit code, and it is suppressed under --quiet. The same detection is available programmatically via collect_removable_ignored_locations():

from complexipy import collect_removable_ignored_locations

removable, failed = collect_removable_ignored_locations(
    paths=["src"],
    exclude=["tests/**"],
    max_complexity_allowed=15,
)
for rem in removable:
    print(f"{rem.path}:{rem.line}  function={rem.function} complexity={rem.complexity}")

docs.title: Migration Guide
docs.text: This page lists, for each major version, the changes that can need action when you upgrade: removed flags and keys with their replacements, and changes to scores and output. Check it before upgrading between major versions.

docs.title: Removed in 7.0.0
docs.text:
The following CLI flags and TOML keys were removed. Use their replacements instead:

Removed flag/key Replacement --output-json / -j --output-format json --output-csv / -c --output-format csv --output-gitlab --output-format gitlab --output-sarif / -sr --output-format sarif --ratchet / -R --diff <ref> (enforces by default) output-json = true output-format = ["json"] output-csv = true output-format = ["csv"] output-gitlab = true output-format = ["gitlab"] output-sarif = true output-format = ["sarif"] ratchet = true [tool.complexipy.diff] branch or --diff <ref> staged = true [tool.complexipy.diff] staged = true details = "low" failed = true

docs.title: What each replacement does
docs.text:
• --output-format <format> selects the machine-readable output format (json, csv, gitlab, sarif). Repeat the flag for multiple formats.
  • --diff <ref> shows a complexity diff against a git reference and enforces the threshold by default.
  • [tool.complexipy.diff] branch sets the default diff reference in TOML; [tool.complexipy.diff] staged = true enables staged comparison by default.
  • failed = true shows only functions above the complexity threshold.

docs.title: Removed in 8.0.0
docs.text:
The CLI was rewritten in Rust. The following old-version compatibility features were removed:

  • Git-URL analysis (complexipy <repository-url>) - local paths only.
  • Legacy cache migration - the previous .complexipy_cache/<hash>.json layout is no longer migrated; existing legacy files are ignored and the delta history starts fresh.
  • Legacy snapshot files - snapshots created with older versions are no longer detected; recreate them with --snapshot-create.
  • -mx short flag - use --max-complexity-allowed instead.

docs.title: Changes in 9.0.0
docs.text:
No flag or key was removed. Scores and some output changed:

  • Scores - this release applies more of the cognitive complexity paper's rules: comprehensions, loop and try else, mixed boolean operators, recursion cycles, nested definitions, and conditional expressions in more places. On the django source tree, 1,946 of 30,813 functions change score: 1,481 go down and 465 go up, and the total of all files drops by 7%. Re-run complexipy and review max-complexity-allowed. If you use a snapshot, recreate it with --snapshot-create, since a function whose score rose fails the check. The changelog lists each rule.
  • --plain output - each line is now <path>:<line> <function> <complexity>. A script that reads the first field as the path must remove the :<line> suffix.
  • Warnings - every CLI warning prints to stderr, including the --diff and --staged warnings, and --quiet no longer hides them. A script that reads these warnings from stdout must read stderr.
  • C005 helper - the extracted predicate no longer carries a -> bool annotation.

docs.title: Refactoring Rules
docs.text: complexipy includes a clippy-inspired refactoring system that provides actionable suggestions for reducing cognitive complexity. Each rule has a unique ID, category, and applicability level.

docs.title: Rule Categories
docs.text: Category Icon Description Complexity ▲ Rules that directly reduce cognitive complexity Readability ◆ Rules that improve code readability

docs.title: Applicability Levels
docs.text:
Level Icon Description Safe to apply * High confidence the generated code is correct as written Needs review ! Usually right, with known failure shapes, so a human must review it Informational i Just guidance, not directly actionable

The level decides how a tool may apply the suggestion:

  • Safe to apply: automatic application (--fix, editor quick fixes) may apply the suggestion directly, when the replacement is also a faithful splice (spliceable).
  • Needs review: automatic application refuses the suggestion unless you opt in explicitly.
  • Informational: nothing ever edits code for it.

No rule uses Needs review today. The level is reserved for a suggestion that is usually right but changes behavior in a known input shape, and a rule may use it only with tests for each known failure shape.

--fix applies a suggestion only at Safe to apply and only when the replacement is a faithful splice. C005 is a splice only when every name its condition reads keeps its value inside a module-level helper (see How --fix applies C005); otherwise its suggestion stays for hand application.

docs.title: Suppressing a Rule
docs.text:
Every rule id can be turned off for a project or for one function. Use --ignore C007 (or ignore = ["C007"] in complexipy.toml) for a project, and # complexipy: ignore[C007] next to a function for one function. --select C001,C007 keeps only the listed rules. A group name selects every rule of that category: --ignore readability hides C005 and C007. An inactive rule never appears in any output. See Rule Selection.

Run complexipy --explain C007 to print a rule's category, applicability, description, and link to its section here.

docs.title: C001: Flatten Nested Conditions
docs.text:
• Category: ▲ Complexity
  • Applicability: i Informational
  • Priority: High (4/5)

Flatten nested condition blocks by using guard clauses with early returns.

docs.title: When does it trigger?
docs.text: This rule triggers when a function has deeply nested if statements (2+ levels of nesting) that add significant complexity.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Before:

def process_data(data):
    if data:
        if data.is_valid():
            if data.is_ready():
                return process(data)
    return None

After:

def process_data(data):
    if not data:
        return None
    if not data.is_valid():
        return None
    if not data.is_ready():
        return None
    return process(data)

docs.title: Why this helps
docs.text: Deeply nested conditions are hard to follow. Using guard clauses with early returns reduces cognitive load by keeping the main path at a lower indentation level.

docs.title: C002: Loop Guards
docs.text:
• Category: ▲ Complexity
  • Applicability: * Safe to apply
  • Priority: Medium (3/5)

Use continue guards at the top of loops to reduce nesting.

docs.title: When does it trigger?
docs.text:
This rule triggers when a loop contains nested if statements that could be converted to early continue guards.

A replacement is offered only when the nested if is the last statement of the loop body. When statements follow it, a guard would skip them, so the rule gives help text instead.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Before:

def process_items(items):
    total = 0
    for item in items:
        if item.active:
            if item.ready:
                total += item.value
    return total

After:

def process_items(items):
    total = 0
    for item in items:
        if not item.active:
            continue
        if not item.ready:
            continue
        total += item.value
    return total

Each guard negates its condition the way a linter expects: x in y becomes x not in y, a is b becomes a is not b, a leading not is dropped, and a name or a call gets a bare not. The not keeps parentheses around and, or, other comparisons, conditional expressions, lambdas, and walrus assignments.

docs.title: Why this helps
docs.text: Nested conditions inside loops add unnecessary indentation. Using continue guards keeps the main logic at a lower nesting level and makes the loop easier to follow.

docs.title: C003: Extract Helper Function
docs.text:
• Category: ▲ Complexity
  • Applicability: i Informational
  • Priority: Low (2/5)

Extract complex code blocks into separate helper functions.

docs.title: When does it trigger?
docs.text: This rule triggers when a code block has high complexity (6+) and spans multiple lines (5+).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Before:

def process_order(order):
    # Complex validation and processing logic
    if order.items:
        for item in order.items:
            if item.quantity > 0:
                if item.price > 0:
                    total = item.quantity * item.price
                    if total > 100:
                        apply_discount(total)
                    process_item(item)

After:

def process_order(order):
    if not order.items:
        return
    for item in order.items:
        process_order_item(item)

def process_order_item(item):
    if item.quantity <= 0 or item.price <= 0:
        return
    total = item.quantity * item.price
    if total > 100:
        apply_discount(total)
    process_item(item)

docs.title: Why this helps
docs.text: Complex code blocks should be extracted into named functions to improve readability and testability. The extracted function can be given a descriptive name that explains its purpose.

docs.title: C004: Split Dispatcher
docs.text:
• Category: ▲ Complexity
  • Applicability: i Informational
  • Priority: Low (2/5)

Split long elif chains into separate handlers.

docs.title: When does it trigger?
docs.text:
This rule triggers when an if/elif chain has 3+ branches. match statements are intentionally excluded: complexipy's cognitive complexity model charges a match a flat cost regardless of how many case clauses it has (unlike an elif chain, where every additional branch adds to the score), so splitting a match into separate handlers would not actually reduce the measured complexity.

The suggested refactor depends on the chain's shape:

  • If every branch compares the same variable against a literal with ==, the chain can become a match statement -- this is recommended over a dispatch dict, since it needs no extra indirection and complexipy's own model scores it as free of the per-branch cost the elif chain has.
  • Otherwise (ranges, multiple variables, non-equality comparisons -- anything a plain match case <value>: can't express) a dispatch dictionary mapping cases to handler functions is suggested instead.

docs.title: Example: single-variable equality → match
docs.text:
Before:

def handle_action(action):
    if action == "create":
        return create_resource()
    elif action == "read":
        return read_resource()
    elif action == "update":
        return update_resource()
    elif action == "delete":
        return delete_resource()
    return None

After:

def handle_action(action):
    match action:
        case "create":
            return create_resource()
        case "read":
            return read_resource()
        case "update":
            return update_resource()
        case "delete":
            return delete_resource()
    return None

docs.title: Example: ranges → dispatch dictionary
docs.text:
Before:

def classify(score):
    if score < 60:
        return "fail"
    elif score < 70:
        return "d"
    elif score < 85:
        return "b"
    elif score < 95:
        return "a"
    return "a+"

After:

def classify(score):
    thresholds = [(60, "fail"), (70, "d"), (85, "b"), (95, "a")]
    for limit, grade in thresholds:
        if score < limit:
            return grade
    return "a+"

docs.title: Why this helps
docs.text: Long conditional chains are hard to maintain and extend. Splitting them into separate handlers -- a match statement when the chain is a simple equality dispatch, a dispatch dictionary otherwise -- makes each case independently testable and the dispatch logic clearer.

docs.title: C011: Flatten Try/Except
docs.text:
• Category: ▲ Complexity
  • Applicability: i Informational
  • Priority: Low (2/5)

Flatten nested try/except blocks by combining or restructuring.

docs.title: When does it trigger?
docs.text: This rule triggers when try/except blocks are nested inside each other.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Before:

def read_config(path):
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            try:
                return json.load(f)
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                return default_config()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return default_config()

After:

def read_config(path):
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            return json.load(f)
    except (FileNotFoundError, json.JSONDecodeError):
        return default_config()

docs.title: Why this helps
docs.text: Nested try/except blocks are confusing and hard to maintain. Consider merging them or extracting the inner block into a separate function with its own error handling.

docs.title: C005: Extract Predicate
docs.text:
• Category: ◆ Readability
  • Applicability: * Safe to apply
  • Priority: Low (2/5)

Extract complex boolean conditions into named predicate functions.

docs.title: When does it trigger?
docs.text:
This rule triggers when a boolean condition contains 2+ logical operators (and, or, not).

The suggestion keeps the statement keyword: an if condition stays an if, a while condition stays a while. Conditions on elif lines only get help text, because an extracted function cannot be placed inside an if-chain.

The extracted helper is emitted at module level with the condition's free variables as parameters (attribute bases included, builtins excluded), so it is unit-testable. The snippet shows the enclosing context at the statement's real indentation, with ... placeholders for skipped statements. Conditions that bind a name with := or contain a lambda/comprehension get help text only.

docs.title: How --fix applies C005
docs.text:
The fix makes two edits. It inserts the helper before the module-level def or class that holds the function, decorators included, and it rewrites the condition's header line into a call to the helper. The suggestion carries the helper in insertions and the header line in replacement, and its reduction is measured.

The call passes every free variable eagerly, while the original condition may skip some of them by short-circuit. So --fix applies C005 only when each name is sure to be bound:

  • a parameter that the function never binds again;
  • a builtin that neither the function, its parameters, nor the module binds;
  • the name of the module-level def or class that holds the function, or a global that a module-level statement binds above the function, outside any if, try, for, while, with, or match, that no module-level del removes, and that no function declares global.

Any other name keeps the snippet for hand application, with spliceable: false. So do a condition inside a nested function or class, a function under a module-level compound statement, a header that spans several lines, and a condition that holds super(), __class__, a private __name, await, or yield.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Before:

def is_eligible(user, order):
    if (user.is_active and user.has_subscription) or (order.total > 100 and not order.is_gift):
        return True
    return False

After:

def is_eligible(user, order):
    return has_active_subscription(user) or is_qualifying_order(order)

def has_active_subscription(user):
    return user.is_active and user.has_subscription

def is_qualifying_order(order):
    return order.total > 100 and not order.is_gift

docs.title: Why this helps
docs.text: Complex boolean expressions are hard to understand at a glance. Extracting them into named predicates makes the code self-documenting and easier to test.

docs.title: C007: Collapsible If
docs.text:
• Category: ◆ Readability
  • Applicability: * Safe to apply
  • Priority: Highest (5/5)

Merge nested if statements into a single if with combined conditions.

docs.title: When does it trigger?
docs.text:
This rule triggers when an if statement's entire body is a single nested if with no else branch, for a chain of two or more such levels.

The merge is skipped when any statement or comment sits between the outer and inner if, so the suggestion never drops code.

A comment on one of the merged if lines, such as # type: ignore, moves to the merged line. When two or more of those lines carry a comment, or the inner if holds its body on the same line, the rule gives help text instead of a replacement.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Before:

def check_eligibility(user):
    if user.is_active:
        if user.has_permission:
            return True
    return False

After:

def check_eligibility(user):
    if user.is_active and user.has_permission:
        return True
    return False

docs.title: Why this helps
docs.text: Nested if statements with a single body can be merged into a single if with combined conditions using and. This reduces nesting and improves readability.

docs.title: Refactor Suggestions
docs.text:
Use --suggest-refactors to print a small, ranked set of deterministic refactor plans next to rich CLI results:

complexipy . --failed --suggest-refactors

Sample output (abbreviated -- the real output also shows a caret-underlined span, the surrounding source, and a documentation link):

      [1] C007 Merge nested if statements
          --> sample.py:4:9
          Category: ◆ Readability | Applicability: * Safe to apply
          Lines 4-6 -> Estimated reduction: -2 complexity (6 -> 4)

          Suggestion: * Safe to apply
          Merge nested conditions into `if item.active and item.ready:`

Plans are based on the Rust AST analysis only; no AI is used and no code is rewritten automatically. Estimated reductions are approximate, ranked, and limited, so treat them as guidance rather than exact future scores. --plain --suggest-refactors prints one line per plan: rule id, title, and reduction.

docs.title: Applying Fixable Suggestions
docs.text:
Use --fix to write the fixable suggestions to the source files. A suggestion is fixable when its applicability is Safe to apply and its replacement is a faithful splice ("spliceable": true in the JSON output). That covers C002 (loop guards), C007 (collapsible if), and C005 (extract predicate) when every name its condition reads keeps its value inside a module-level helper. For C005 the fix also inserts the helper above the function (see How --fix applies C005).

complexipy . --fix

--fix changes only functions whose complexity is above max-complexity-allowed, the same rule the gate uses. Every pass checks the threshold again, so a function stops changing once it passes. A function at or under the threshold keeps its suggestions in the report and is never rewritten. One run applies every fixable plan of those functions in every analyzed file and repeats pass by pass, up to 8 passes, until no fixable plan remains; a later pass labels its diff pass 2:. For each fixed file the run prints a syntax-highlighted unified diff of the applied changes, with line numbers, one context line per hunk, and the rule that fired, and then a summary of fixed and skipped fixes. The summary shows the reduction per fix as (-3 complexity), with a tilde before the number ((- ~3 complexity)) when the number is estimated. Summary lines use the file's line numbers from before the run, in every pass; a fix inside a region that an earlier pass rewrote reports that region's lines. When nothing is fixable the run prints No fixes to apply. The report and every gate measure the state after the fixes. Re-analyzing a fixed file shows the finding is gone and the complexity dropped by the plan's measured reduction.

--fix --dry-run previews the same changes: it prints only the unified diff and writes nothing, not even the cache or the snapshot. --fix runs wherever you are: uncommitted changes, untracked files, and a missing git repository never block it, and no extra flag is needed. A fix keeps the file's line endings and its trailing newline. Per-rule filtering rides on --select and --ignore.

--fix rewrites only regular files inside the directory it runs from. It skips a symlink, and a file that changed on disk after complexipy read it. It writes a new file next to the original and renames it into place, keeping the permission bits and the group but not setuid, setgid, extended attributes, or ACLs.

JSON Output Structure:

[
    {
        "path": "src/main.py",
        "file_name": "main.py",
        "function_name": "process_data",
        "complexity": 6,
        "line_start": 1,
        "line_end": 7,
        "line_complexities": [
            {"line": 3, "complexity": 1},
            {"line": 4, "complexity": 2},
            {"line": 5, "complexity": 3}
        ],
        "refactor_plans": [
            {
                "rule_id": "C007",
                "kind": "collapsible_if",
                "title": "Merge nested if statements",
                "line_start": 4,
                "line_end": 6,
                "column_start": 9,
                "current_complexity": 6,
                "estimated_reduction": 2,
                "estimated_complexity_after": 4,
                "reduction_is_measured": true,
                "category": "Readability",
                "applicability": "MachineApplicable",
                "description": "Merge nested if statements into a single if with combined conditions",
                "explanation": "Nested if statements with a single body can be merged into a single if with combined conditions using 'and'. This reduces nesting and improves readability.",
                "references": [],
                "suggestion": {
                    "replacement": "        if item.active and item.ready:\n            total += item.value",
                    "applicability": "MachineApplicable",
                    "spliceable": true,
                    "insertions": [],
                    "description": "Merge nested conditions into `if item.active and item.ready:`"
                },
                "help": null,
                "doc_url": "https://complexipy.com/refactoring-rules/#c007-collapsible-if"
            }
        ]
    }
]

JSON output contains one entry per emitted function. The refactor_plans list is only populated when --suggest-refactors is also passed -- otherwise it's [], matching the CLI's rich-output behavior. CSV output does not include plans, and a cell that a spreadsheet would run as a formula (one that starts with =, +, -, or @) is written with a leading '. Each JSON entry carries the function's line_start and line_end, and line_complexities: the lines that add to the score, one entry per line in line order, whose complexity values sum to the function's complexity. CSV output does not include line data.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
# Show refactoring suggestions
complexipy . --suggest-refactors

# Show suggestions for failing functions only
complexipy . --failed --suggest-refactors

# Export suggestions to JSON
complexipy . --output-format json --suggest-refactors

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from complexipy import code_complexity

code = """
def process(data):
    if data:
        if data.is_valid():
            return process(data)
    return None
"""

result = code_complexity(code)
for func in result.functions:
    for plan in func.refactor_plans:
        print(f"[{plan.rule_id}] {plan.title}")
        print(f"  Category: {plan.category}")
        print(f"  Applicability: {plan.applicability}")
        print(f"  Reduction: -{plan.estimated_reduction} complexity")
        if plan.suggestion:
            print(f"  Suggested replacement:\n{plan.suggestion.replacement}")
        elif plan.help:
            print(f"  Help: {plan.help}")
        print(f"  Docs: {plan.doc_url}")

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text:
The JSON output includes all rule metadata for programmatic consumption:

{
  "rule_id": "C007",
  "kind": "collapsible_if",
  "title": "Merge nested if statements",
  "category": "Readability",
  "applicability": "MachineApplicable",
  "description": "Merge nested if statements into a single if with combined conditions",
  "line_start": 3,
  "line_end": 5,
  "column_start": 5,
  "current_complexity": 4,
  "estimated_reduction": 1,
  "estimated_complexity_after": 3,
  "reduction_is_measured": true,
  "suggestion": {
    "replacement": "    if data and data.is_valid():\n        return process(data)",
    "applicability": "MachineApplicable",
    "spliceable": true,
    "insertions": [],
    "description": "Merge nested conditions into `if data and data.is_valid():`"
  },
  "help": null,
  "explanation": "Nested if statements with a single body can be merged into a single if with combined conditions using 'and'. This reduces nesting and improves readability.",
  "references": [],
  "doc_url": "https://complexipy.com/refactoring-rules/#c007-collapsible-if"
}

docs.title: Measured vs estimated reductions
docs.text:
Every plan reports how much applying it lowers the complexity (estimated_reduction / estimated_complexity_after) together with a confidence flag, reduction_is_measured:

  • Measured (true): the rule spliced its suggestion into the real source, re-parsed it, and re-ran the scorer. The number is the literal answer to "apply this and re-score" - exactly what C002, C007, and a spliceable C005 report, since they carry machine-applicable replacements. The CLI shows these without a qualifier: Reduction: -2 complexity (7 -> 5).
  • Estimated (false): the number comes from the rule's hand-derived formula (help-only rules C001, C003, C004, C011, a C005 snippet that is not spliceable, plus any fallback when a splice cannot be re-parsed). The CLI renders these with a tilde: Estimated reduction: ~-2 complexity (7 -> 5).

A measured reduction of 0 means the suggestion does not actually lower complexity; the plan is dropped rather than shown.

docs.title: Rule ID Reference
docs.text: ID Name Category Applicability Priority C001 Flatten Nested Conditions ▲ Complexity i Informational High C002 Loop Guards ▲ Complexity * Safe to apply Medium C003 Extract Helper Function ▲ Complexity i Informational Low C004 Split Dispatcher ▲ Complexity i Informational Low C005 Extract Predicate ◆ Readability * Safe to apply Low C007 Collapsible If ◆ Readability * Safe to apply Highest C011 Flatten Try/Except ▲ Complexity i Informational Low

docs.title: What Do the Numbers Mean?
docs.text: Cognitive complexity scores represent the mental effort required to understand a piece of code. Higher scores indicate code that is more difficult to comprehend and maintain.

docs.title: Recommended Thresholds
docs.text:
Score Range Interpretation Recommendation 0-5 Simple Easy to understand, no action needed 6-10 Moderate Generally acceptable, but watch for further growth 11-15 Complex Consider refactoring if functionality is being added 16-25 High Refactoring recommended 26+ Very High Refactoring strongly recommended

Default Threshold

complexipy uses a default threshold of 15. Functions exceeding this score will trigger warnings.

docs.title: How Complexity is Calculated
docs.text: Cognitive complexity is calculated by analyzing the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) of your Python code and applying these rules:

docs.title: 1. Base Complexity Increments
docs.text:
Each control flow structure adds to the complexity:

Structure Score Example if statement +1 if condition: elif clause +1 elif other_condition: else clause +1 else: after if, for, while, or try (no nesting increment; its body is nested) for loop +1 for item in items: while loop +1 while condition: except handler +1 except ValueError: finally clause +0 finally: (its body is not nested) Ternary operator +1 x if condition else y Comprehension clause +0 [x for x in xs if x]

docs.title: 2. Nesting Multiplier
docs.text:
This is the key innovation: nested structures add extra complexity based on their depth.

def example():
    if a:           # +1 (base)
        if b:       # +2 (1 base + 1 nesting)
            if c:   # +3 (1 base + 2 nesting)
                pass
# Total complexity: 6

The formula is: complexity = 1 + nesting_level

docs.title: 3. Boolean Operators
docs.text:
Complex logical conditions increase cognitive load:

# Score: 3
def check(a, b, c):
    if a and b or c:  # +1 (if) +2 (boolean operators)
        return True
  • Each run of like operators, read left to right: +1
  • Each change between and and or starts a new run: a or b and c or d reads or, and, or and scores +3

docs.title: 4. Special Cases
docs.text:
Break and Continue

# Score: 3
for item in items:  # +1
    if condition:   # +2 (1 + nesting)
        break       # +0 (no additional score)

Match Statements (Python 3.10+)

# Score: 5
match value:        # +1
    case 1:
        if x:       # +2 (1 + nesting)
            pass
    case 2:
        if y:       # +2 (1 + nesting)
            pass

Recursion Each function in a recursion cycle adds +1 once, however many recursive calls it makes. The cycle can be direct (fact calls fact) or indirect (a calls b, b calls a). The +1 of a nested function, or of a method of a class nested in a function, goes to the function that holds it. A call counts when it resolves in the same file: a bare name to each def of the nearest enclosing function or module scope that binds it, when every other binding of the name in that scope (a parameter, assignment, walrus, for or with target, except ... as name, match capture, del, import, type alias, or class) has always run before that def binds it and none is made through a global or nonlocal declaration (the binding comes earlier in the code, in another branch of the same if or match, or in an except handler of a try whose body runs nothing after the def, and in a loop that repeats both it runs earlier in every pass: the def does not sit in an if or other block of its own in the loop, no break or continue comes between them, no try or with is around the loop, and the binding is not in a while test), self.m() and cls.m() to a method of the caller's class (a closure in a method uses that method's self), or K.m() to a method of class K when the name K resolves the same way to exactly one class of the file and every other binding of K in that scope has always run before the class binds it, by the same order rule as a def (a star import or a type parameter in that scope, or a binding made through a global or nonlocal declaration, leaves the call unresolved). A call through K in the decorators, bases, or body of class K itself does not resolve to it, since the class has not bound its name yet. A call inside a lambda, or in the decorators, default arguments, bases, or class body of a nested definition, counts for the function that holds it. A lambda's own parameters, a comprehension's loop variables, and the type parameters of a class or function hide outer names where they are visible. A call in a class body to a name that the same class body binds goes to the module's binding when the call runs before that binding, and to the class's binding after it; when the order cannot be known from the code, such as a binding inside an if or a loop, the call adds nothing. A bare decorator such as @f is not a call, so it does not count. Calls through super(), other objects, or imports do not count, nor does a method that K only inherits, and cycles across files are not detected.

Decorators A function whose body is only a nested def and a return does not raise the nesting level of the nested function, as the paper's Python decorator exception says. The return must give back the nested function: by name (return inner), or as a direct argument of a call (return functools.wraps(f)(inner), return update_wrapper(inner, f)). Two choices differ from the paper's wording, which allows any return and names nothing else. A call of the nested function, such as return inner(), does not qualify: it runs the nested function instead of handing it back, so the function is not a decorator. A leading docstring is allowed: it documents the decorator and adds no control flow. Any other statement removes the exception. The expressions in the return still count.

Python constructs the paper does not name

  • Comprehensions: the for and if clauses add nothing and do not raise the nesting level. The paper ignores shorthand that lets several statements be written readably as one, and a comprehension is shorthand for a loop that builds a value. A ternary or a boolean operator inside a comprehension still counts.
  • else on for, while, and try: +1, with no nesting increment, and its body raises the nesting level, like else after if. The else body runs only when the loop ends without break or the try body raised nothing, so it is a branch the reader must track. The paper calls else a hybrid increment: no nesting increment, but a higher nesting level for what it holds.
  • case guards: +0 for the guard itself. A boolean operator sequence or a ternary inside it counts, at the nesting level of the match. The paper gives a switch and all its cases a single increment and does not name guards, so a guard is read as part of its case.
  • Mixed boolean operators: the operators of one condition are read left to right, as they appear in the code, and each change between and and or starts a new sequence. A not starts a new condition for its operand.

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Sequential Logic
docs.text:
def process_user(user):
    if not user:              # +1
        return None

    if user.is_active:        # +1
        send_welcome_email()

    if user.needs_verification: # +1
        send_verification()

    return user
# Total complexity: 3

Analysis: Three sequential if statements, no nesting. Easy to follow.

docs.title: Example 2: Nested Logic
docs.text:
def validate_order(order):
    if order:                        # +1
        if order.items:              # +2 (1 + nesting)
            for item in order.items: # +3 (1 + nesting)
                if item.quantity > 0: # +4 (1 + nesting)
                    process(item)
    return False
# Total complexity: 10

Analysis: Deep nesting creates exponential growth in cognitive load.

docs.title: Example 3: Complex Conditions
docs.text:
def check_eligibility(user, product):
    if user.age >= 18 and user.verified and product.available: # +2
        #  ^^^ if: +1, and run: +1, total: +2
        return True
    return False
# Total complexity: 2

Analysis: Multiple boolean operators increase the mental load of understanding the condition.

docs.title: Example 4: Exception Handling
docs.text:
def load_config(path):
    try:                              # try itself: +0
        with open(path) as f:         # +0 (with adds nothing and does not nest)
            data = json.load(f)
            if validate(data):        # +1 (try and with bodies are not nested)
                return data
    except FileNotFoundError:         # +1
        create_default_config()
    except json.JSONDecodeError:      # +1
        log_error()
    finally:                          # +0 (finally itself)
        if log_enabled:               # +1
            log("Config load attempted")
# Total complexity: 4

docs.title: What Should I Refactor?
docs.text:
Focus on functions with scores above your threshold (default: 15). Common refactoring strategies:

  1. Extract Methods - Pull nested logic into separate functions
  2. Early Returns - Use guard clauses to reduce nesting
  3. Simplify Conditions - Break complex boolean expressions into named variables
  4. Strategy Pattern - Replace nested if/else with polymorphism

docs.title: Example Refactoring
docs.text:
Before (Complexity: 13)

def process_order(order):
    if order:                          # +1
        if order.is_valid():           # +2
            if order.payment:          # +3
                if order.payment.process(): # +4
                    ship_order(order)
                else:                          # +1 (else clause)
                    refund(order)
            else:                      # +1 (else clause)
                notify_payment_required()
        else:                          # +1 (else clause)
            log_invalid_order()
    return False

After (Complexity: 4)

def process_order(order):
    if not order:                  # +1
        return False

    if not order.is_valid():       # +1
        log_invalid_order()
        return False

    if not order.payment:          # +1
        notify_payment_required()
        return False

    if order.payment.process():    # +1
        ship_order(order)
        return True

    refund(order)
    return False

Key improvements:

  • Reduced nesting from 4 levels to 1
  • Complexity dropped from 13 to 4
  • Logic is now linear and easier to follow

docs.title: Score Interpretation Tips
docs.text:
1. Context Matters - A score of 20 might be acceptable for a complex algorithm but problematic for business logic
  2. Trend Over Time - Watch for increasing complexity in functions you modify frequently
  3. Relative Scores - Compare functions within the same codebase to identify outliers
  4. Team Agreement - Establish thresholds that work for your team and project
